vignette:
She is a 38-year-old Middle Eastern woman who works as a housekeeper, married, and accustomed to carrying the rhythm of other people’s homes on her back. Before the assault, she describes herself as someone who kept moving, kept cleaning, kept going. Her days were built around routines she could control: making beds, folding laundry, scrubbing kitchens until surfaces shone. She took pride in her work, not because it was visible, but because it was steady and because it allowed her to contribute to her family. She speaks of her marriage as caring and familiar, though since the assault she feels herself withdrawing even from her husband, as if there is a pane of glass between them.

The assault happens abruptly, in a moment that still feels to her unreal when she tries to speak about it. She had been returning from work, tired and thinking about dinner and the small errands waiting at home. What she remembers most is how quickly ordinary life changes shape. One minute she is walking, preoccupied with the next task; the next, she is in danger, trying to understand what is happening while her body seems to separate from her mind. She describes freezing, then fighting to get away, then later feeling ashamed that she could not do more. In the days that follow, she keeps replaying the event in fragments, unable to make it feel complete, as though her memory has been broken into pieces she cannot arrange.

At first she assumes she will recover if she stays busy. She returns to work, but the homes she cleans no longer feel neutral. Certain smells—a heavy cologne, bleach, warm laundry, stale food in a sink—can pull her back without warning. Her body reacts before her thoughts do. Her shoulders tighten, her breathing shortens, and she becomes acutely aware of where exits are, what shadows are in hallways, whether a door is locked behind her. She notices herself scanning constantly, even in safe places, and she hates how tired that makes her. She used to move through houses efficiently; now she feels as if every room might contain a threat.

Sleep becomes one of the first things to unravel. At night, she lies beside her husband and listens for sounds in the apartment, unable to settle. She falls asleep late and wakes often, sometimes from dreams so vivid that she wakes already crying, her heart racing, convinced for a few seconds that the assault is happening again. In the mornings she feels unrefreshed and irritable, and she struggles to keep herself focused while working. On some days she forgets simple things—where she left a rag, whether she already wiped a counter, which bus stop to take—and this frightens her because she has always prided herself on being dependable.

She begins to avoid anything that reminds her of what happened. She changes the route she takes home. She no longer likes being alone outside after dark. If a stranger walks too close behind her, she crosses the street or stops until they pass. She no longer watches certain television programs and turns away from news stories about violence. Even in her own home, she feels less comfortable in dark rooms or when the apartment is quiet. Her husband tries to reassure her, but reassurance does not reach the part of her that is always braced for impact. She loves him and feels guilty that she cannot be touched easily. When he reaches for her unexpectedly, her whole body tenses, and she hates the flash of panic that rises before she can stop it.

She also feels a deep, complicated anger—at the assailant, at herself, at the unfairness of having to carry the afterlife of someone else’s violence. Some days the anger turns inward. She asks herself why she was there, why she did not run sooner, why she still cannot “get over it.” Other days she feels numb, as though she is watching her own life from a distance. At work she can appear calm and competent, but internally she is often counting minutes until she can leave. She says she feels split between the part of her that keeps functioning and the part that remains stuck at the moment of the attack.

Over time, she has become more isolated. She declines invitations, speaks less with friends, and finds it hard to explain why she seems different. She worries that others will think she is weak or damaged. At the same time, she feels a persistent need to stay vigilant, as if vigilance might prevent another terrible thing from happening. Even now, months later, she continues to live as though danger could appear at any time. The world feels narrower, less forgiving, and she moves through it carefully, carrying her fear in her body while trying to preserve the ordinary life she had before.
